text: PREFACE After Canon Bouch had for some time been collecting material for a social and economic history of the Lake Counties, on lines parallel to his People and Prelates (1948), it became clear that ill- health would prevent him from finishing the work himself and he honoured me in 1955 by an invitation to collaborate in what remained to be done.
text_raw:
PREFACE 
After Canon Bouch had for some time been collecting material 
for a social and economic history of the Lake Counties, on lines 
parallel to his People and Prelates (1948), it became clear that ill- 
health would prevent him from finishing the work himself and 
he honoured me in 1955 by an invitation to collaborate in what 
remained to be done.

text: That meant some extension and modifica¬ tion of the parts already drafted, roughly the first three chapters of the present volume, adding to the material set in order for later chapters, more especially parts of the present chapters IV, VI, VII, VIII and XII, and adding also the parts towards which very little had been gathered, particularly the present chapters V, IX, X and XIII.
text_raw:
That meant some extension and modifica¬ 
tion of the parts already drafted, roughly the first three chapters of 
the present volume, adding to the material set in order for later 
chapters, more especially parts of the present chapters IV, VI, 
VII, VIII and XII, and adding also the parts towards which very 
little had been gathered, particularly the present chapters V, IX, 
X and XIII.

text: The chapters were drafted, discussed, re-drafted and revised one by one; but, unfortunately, as Canon Bouch’s health grew worse he became less and less able to apply the critical powers by which the earlier chapters had been improved, and he died in July, 1959, without seeing the work in the form submitted for publication.
text_raw:
The chapters were drafted, discussed, re-drafted and 
revised one by one; but, unfortunately, as Canon Bouch’s health 
grew worse he became less and less able to apply the critical 
powers by which the earlier chapters had been improved, and he 
died in July, 1959, without seeing the work in the form submitted 
for publication.

text: It is hoped, nevertheless, that the book is sub¬ stantially what he would have wished it to be.

text: EARLY HISTORY OF THE LAKE COUNTIES Improved highways in the eighteenth century, railways in the nineteenth and motor roads in our own day have made accessible to many thousands of people every year Lakeland valleys formerly remote and almost entirely unvisited.
text_raw:
EARLY HISTORY OF THE LAKE COUNTIES 
Improved highways in the eighteenth century, railways in the 
nineteenth and motor roads in our own day have made accessible 
to many thousands of people every year Lakeland valleys formerly 
remote and almost entirely unvisited.

text: As a consequence, not only have visitors poured into the region but the inhabitants of the region itself have become much more closely involved, for good or ill, in the life of the nation at large, and much less different than they used to be, in speech, dress, habits and belief, from the population of England in general.
text_raw:
As a consequence, not only 
have visitors poured into the region but the inhabitants of the 
region itself have become much more closely involved, for good 
or ill, in the life of the nation at large, and much less different than 
they used to be, in speech, dress, habits and belief, from the 
population of England in general.

text: There are, indeed, vestiges of the old order still to be found, but the society and way of life with which we are concerned in this volume have in their essentials vanished, not, as a rule, suddenly or violently but by gradual adaptation to new conditions, under influences arising partly within that society itself and partly from outside it.
text_raw:
There are, indeed, vestiges of 
the old order still to be found, but the society and way of life 
with which we are concerned in this volume have in their 
essentials vanished, not, as a rule, suddenly or violently but by 
gradual adaptation to new conditions, under influences arising 
partly within that society itself and partly from outside it.

text: Our main endeavour is to describe the life of the Lake Counties and the changes in it from the eve of the Reformation to the eve of the 1832 Reform Act, and we leave to other hands the difficult task of adequately writing the economic and social history of medieval Lakeland; but, since the institutions of one age com¬ monly survive into another, we think it necessary, in order that sixteenth-century conditions should be better understood, to give some account of the district and its inhabitants in darker and more distant times.
text_raw:
Our 
main endeavour is to describe the life of the Lake Counties and 
the changes in it from the eve of the Reformation to the eve of 
the 1832 Reform Act, and we leave to other hands the difficult 
task of adequately writing the economic and social history of 
medieval Lakeland; but, since the institutions of one age com¬ 
monly survive into another, we think it necessary, in order 
that sixteenth-century conditions should be better understood, 
to give some account of the district and its inhabitants in darker 
and more distant times.

text: EARLY HISTORY OF THE LAKE COUNTIES 13 wealth but more than peasant status’.1 In Gospatric’s charter, rela¬ ting to Allerdale, cheng, according to one authority, means ‘a landowner who did not enjoy the full rights of a free man’:2 according to another, the dreng should be regarded as a man ‘whose freedom of person and tenure had neither been affirmed nor denied by Saxon custom’.3 The instances of this tenure so far known in our region are mainly confined to an area stretching from Soulby and Asby in the south to Glassonby and Gamblesby in the north,4 though there are instances, too, in Hensingham, about 1140, and Ribton, near Bridekirk, in the early thirteenth century.5 The distribution suggests that the tenure may have been associated with a people coming into the region from the east by way of the Stainmore gap, and settling to the west and north¬ west of the road by which they came.

wealth but more than peasant status’.1 In Gospatric’s charter, rela¬

text: 16 THE LAKE COUNTIES, I5OO-183O have slain a smaller proportion in the north than in the south.1 Even if that were not so, our region suffered, as the south did not, from a deadlier enemy. ‘A Scots raid down towards Tyneside’, as Sir John Clapham said, ‘often did as much killing in relation to local population as the plague did nearly everywhere; the plague did not burn crops or houses but the Scots (and in reverse the English) did’.2 The persistent raiding was indeed sufficiently disastrous to persuade the government to remit the tax arrears of Cumberland, Westmorland and Northumberland in 1389 and to grant exemption from a tax in 1488.3 Population and its Distribution To trace in any detail the fortunes of the Lake Counties during the troubled fourteenth and fifteenth centuries is not part of the limited task we have set ourselves in this volume, but it is relevant to attempt a description of their condition towards the close of the Middle Ages, and to that end it is desirable to have some idea how many people they contained.
text_raw:
16 THE LAKE COUNTIES, I5OO-183O 
have slain a smaller proportion in the north than in the south.1 
Even if that were not so, our region suffered, as the south did not, 
from a deadlier enemy. ‘A Scots raid down towards Tyneside’, 
as Sir John Clapham said, ‘often did as much killing in relation to 
local population as the plague did nearly everywhere; the plague 
did not burn crops or houses but the Scots (and in reverse the 
English) did’.2 The persistent raiding was indeed sufficiently 
disastrous to persuade the government to remit the tax arrears 
of Cumberland, Westmorland and Northumberland in 1389 and 
to grant exemption from a tax in 1488.3 
Population and its Distribution 
To trace in any detail the fortunes of the Lake Counties during 
the troubled fourteenth and fifteenth centuries is not part of the 
limited task we have set ourselves in this volume, but it is relevant 
to attempt a description of their condition towards the close of 
the Middle Ages, and to that end it is desirable to have some idea 
how many people they contained.

text: Other medieval roads3 were the ‘street’ from Appleby to Tebay, the Brampton ‘streitte’ to Appleby and the ‘great street’ (1magna strata) from Kendal to Shap mentioned in an early thir¬ teenth-century deed.4 That may have been made by the monks; it was certainly useful to them and to the travellers for whom they provided accommodation in a bleak and scantily populated part of the country.5 In north-west Cumberland there was an ‘ordi¬ nary road through Bassenthwaite’ mentioned in a grant to Flolm Cultram Abbey about 1317.6 There must have been other roads as well, to bring cattle to such towns as Egremont and Cocker- mouth, and, for instance, to bring the loads of timber needed for repairs to the castle in the latter place in 1322-3.7 Similarly the monks of Holm Cultram, having the right to dig iron ore in Coupland, to take dead wood in Allerdale and to work a forge at Whinfell, near Lorton,8 must have had means and routes for the transport of ore, fuel and iron.

chapter_title: part m, 459-98, 507-8. For a list of Lake District place-names see LDH 81-101!
text: The Large Houses of the Lake Counties1 Throughout the period under review the large house was divided into three separate parts: a place for sleeping, a place for eating and a place for storage and preparation.
text_raw:
The Large Houses of the Lake Counties1 
Throughout the period under review the large house was 
divided into three separate parts: a place for sleeping, a place for 
eating and a place for storage and preparation.

chapter_title: part m, 459-98, 507-8. For a list of Lake District place-names see LDH 81-101!
text: The sleeping place, bower, was private, being set apart for the master of the house and his family.

chapter_title: part m, 459-98, 507-8. For a list of Lake District place-names see LDH 81-101!

the household and contained the principal fireplace.

chapter_title: part m, 459-98, 507-8. For a list of Lake District place-names see LDH 81-101!
text: The storage place or service room accommodated in addition to supplies the functions of cleaning and preparation too dirty for the hall.
text_raw:
The storage 
place or service room accommodated in addition to supplies the

chapter_title: part m, 459-98, 507-8. For a list of Lake District place-names see LDH 81-101!
text: At first, each part was housed in one room, the three being arranged vertically in tower houses and horizontally in manor houses; but as wealth and security increased each function was spread over several rooms, bedrooms, parlours, living-rooms, kitchens, sculleries and cellars, and these rooms too were distributed both horizontally like the manor houses and vertically like the towers.
text_raw:
At 
first, each part was housed in one room, the three being arranged 
vertically in tower houses and horizontally in manor houses; but 
as wealth and security increased each function was spread over 
several rooms, bedrooms, parlours, living-rooms, kitchens, 
sculleries and cellars, and these rooms too were distributed both 
horizontally like the manor houses and vertically like the towers.

chapter_title: part m, 459-98, 507-8. For a list of Lake District place-names see LDH 81-101!
text: During the period of recurrent conflict between England and Scotland, occupiers of houses in the Border counties tried to rnake them impregnable, like the castles, by the strength of their fortifications or else constructed them lightly so that they could easily be rebuilt.

During the period of recurrent conflict between England and 
Scotland, occupiers of houses in the Border counties tried to 
rnake them impregnable, like the castles, by the strength of their 
fortifications or else constructed them lightly so that they could 
easily be rebuilt.

chapter_title: part m, 459-98, 507-8. For a list of Lake District place-names see LDH 81-101!
text: EARLY HISTORY OP THE LAKE COUNTIES 33 The large house in the Border counties had therefore to provide living quarters for normal times, a tower of refuge in time of danger, a base for agriculture and a protected corral for stock and crops.
text_raw:
EARLY HISTORY OP THE LAKE COUNTIES 33 
The large house in the Border counties had therefore to provide 
living quarters for normal times, a tower of refuge in time of 
danger, a base for agriculture and a protected corral for stock 
and crops.

chapter_title: part m, 459-98, 507-8. For a list of Lake District place-names see LDH 81-101!
text: Only when the Border had been completely pacified could development of the large house on the same lines as in other parts of the country be resumed.
text_raw:
Only when the Border had been completely pacified 
could development of the large house on the same lines as in 
other parts of the country be resumed.

chapter_title: part m, 459-98, 507-8. For a list of Lake District place-names see LDH 81-101!
text: In Cumberland and Westmorland five zones of settlement can be distinguished.
text_raw:
In Cumberland and Westmorland five zones of settlement can 
be distinguished.

chapter_title: part m, 459-98, 507-8. For a list of Lake District place-names see LDH 81-101!
text: On the Border, where population was sparse, the large houses were generally fortified and set in isolation, though often within sight of each other.
text_raw:
On the Border, where population was sparse, 
the large houses were generally fortified and set in isolation, 
though often within sight of each other.

chapter_title: part m, 459-98, 507-8. For a list of Lake District place-names see LDH 81-101!
text: The Eden valley was more populous and houses around the forest wastes and along the line where cultivated land met the open fell were fortified, but in the heart of the valley fortification was slight.
text_raw:
The Eden valley was 
more populous and houses around the forest wastes and along the 
line where cultivated land met the open fell were fortified, but 
in the heart of the valley fortification was slight.

chapter_title: part m, 459-98, 507-8. For a list of Lake District place-names see LDH 81-101!
text: The dales of the Lake District proper were sparsely settled, but the inhabitants could rely on remoteness for protection.
text_raw:
The dales of 
the Lake District proper were sparsely settled, but the inhabitants 
could rely on remoteness for protection.

chapter_title: part m, 459-98, 507-8. For a list of Lake District place-names see LDH 81-101!
text: Along the sea coast protection against raiders was necessary as on the Border.
text_raw:
Along the sea coast 
protection against raiders was necessary as on the Border.

chapter_title: part m, 459-98, 507-8. For a list of Lake District place-names see LDH 81-101!
text: Only in the valleys of the Kent and the Lune was the design of the large house generally free from the needs of defence.
text_raw:
Only 
in the valleys of the Kent and the Lune was the design of the 
large house generally free from the needs of defence.

chapter_title: part m, 459-98, 507-8. For a list of Lake District place-names see LDH 81-101!
text: The basis of the medieval settlement appears to have been the ‘barmkin’, a sort of corral, where, behind a timber fence, cattle and dependents could shelter, defended by the menfolk.
text_raw:
The basis of the medieval settlement appears to have been the 
‘barmkin’, a sort of corral, where, behind a timber fence, cattle 
and dependents could shelter, defended by the menfolk.

chapter_title: part m, 459-98, 507-8. For a list of Lake District place-names see LDH 81-101!
text: The barmkin corresponds to the bailey of the medieval castle.
text_raw:
The 
barmkin corresponds to the bailey of the medieval castle.

chapter_title: part m, 459-98, 507-8. For a list of Lake District place-names see LDH 81-101!
text: It could be easily erected and replaced if destroyed, but, being difficult to defend and without protection against fire, it often perished.
text_raw:
It could 
be easily erected and replaced if destroyed, but, being difficult to 
defend and without protection against fire, it often perished.

chapter_title: part m, 459-98, 507-8. For a list of Lake District place-names see LDH 81-101!
text: No example has survived intact.
text_raw:
No 
example has survived intact.

chapter_title: part m, 459-98, 507-8. For a list of Lake District place-names see LDH 81-101!
text: Better protection to human life was given by the timber tower or the palisade of timber ‘piles’.
text_raw:
Better protection to human life was 
given by the timber tower or the palisade of timber ‘piles’.

chapter_title: part m, 459-98, 507-8. For a list of Lake District place-names see LDH 81-101!
text: This corresponds rather to the motte of a Norman castle, though there does not usually appear to have been much of a mound.
text_raw:
This 
corresponds rather to the motte of a Norman castle, though there 
does not usually appear to have been much of a mound.

chapter_title: part m, 459-98, 507-8. For a list of Lake District place-names see LDH 81-101!
text: The timber tower, like the barmkin, was easily constructed and re¬ placed, but could be better defended.
text_raw:
The 
timber tower, like the barmkin, was easily constructed and re¬ 
placed, but could be better defended.

chapter_title: part m, 459-98, 507-8. For a list of Lake District place-names see LDH 81-101!
text: It too was susceptible to attack by fire and none has survived though there are references to such towers in literature.
text_raw:
It too was susceptible to 
attack by fire and none has survived though there are references 
to such towers in literature.

chapter_title: part m, 459-98, 507-8. For a list of Lake District place-names see LDH 81-101!
text: In those parts of Scotland whose history and topography were similar to those of the Lake Counties there are known to have been towers of clay-protected or mass-clay construction.
text_raw:
In those parts of Scotland whose history and topography were 
similar to those of the Lake Counties there are known to have 
been towers of clay-protected or mass-clay construction.

chapter_title: part m, 459-98, 507-8. For a list of Lake District place-names see LDH 81-101!
text: By means of a thick daub of clay a timber tower could be made more resistant to fire and, incidentally, better protected against bad

chapter_title: part m, 459-98, 507-8. For a list of Lake District place-names see LDH 81-101!
text: A mass-clay tower would be even safer and more com¬ fortable, but it is unlikely that more than two storeys would be attempted in this construction.
text_raw:
A mass-clay tower would be even safer and more com¬ 
fortable, but it is unlikely that more than two storeys would be 
attempted in this construction.

chapter_title: part m, 459-98, 507-8. For a list of Lake District place-names see LDH 81-101!
text: No examples, indeed, survive in Cumberland or Westmorland, but the use until recent times of clay in house construction in various parts of the region, and references to clay in house names in other parts, suggest that the Scottish methods may well have been used here.
text_raw:
No examples, indeed, survive in 
Cumberland or Westmorland, but the use until recent times of 
clay in house construction in various parts of the region, and 
references to clay in house names in other parts, suggest that the 
Scottish methods may well have been used here.

chapter_title: part m, 459-98, 507-8. For a list of Lake District place-names see LDH 81-101!
text: The earhest surviving large houses are of the pele tower form, i.e. three units arranged vertically in a defensive structure of fire- resisting stone.
text_raw:
The earhest surviving large houses are of the pele tower form, 
i.e. three units arranged vertically in a defensive structure of fire- 
resisting stone.

chapter_title: part m, 459-98, 507-8. For a list of Lake District place-names see LDH 81-101!
text: Many such were built in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries and they formed the basis for developments in design and construction in the succeeding centuries.
text_raw:
Many such were built in the fourteenth and 
fifteenth centuries and they formed the basis for developments 
in design and construction in the succeeding centuries.

chapter_title: part m, 459-98, 507-8. For a list of Lake District place-names see LDH 81-101!
text: The typical pele tower had three storeys, a store room on the ground floor, without windows and ventilated only by small holes in the walls, a hall on the first floor with a fireplace and some small windows, and a bower on the second floor.
text_raw:
The 
typical pele tower had three storeys, a store room on the ground 
floor, without windows and ventilated only by small holes in the 
walls, a hall on the first floor with a fireplace and some small 
windows, and a bower on the second floor.

chapter_title: part m, 459-98, 507-8. For a list of Lake District place-names see LDH 81-101!
text: On the roof was a flat fighting deck, or provision was made for timber brattishing to project from a parapet.
text_raw:
On the roof was a 
flat fighting deck, or provision was made for timber brattishing 
to project from a parapet.

chapter_title: part m, 459-98, 507-8. For a list of Lake District place-names see LDH 81-101!
text: Defence was mainly passive, depending on the solidity and fire resistance of the stone, the strength of the iron reinforcement of the small door and the height of the window openings above the ground, but even such passive defence would generally be adequate against lightly equipped raiders.
text_raw:
Defence was mainly passive, depending 
on the solidity and fire resistance of the stone, the strength of the 
iron reinforcement of the small door and the height of the window 
openings above the ground, but even such passive defence would 
generally be adequate against lightly equipped raiders.

chapter_title: part m, 459-98, 507-8. For a list of Lake District place-names see LDH 81-101!
text: The distri¬ bution of pele towers clearly shows the areas of vulnerability.
text_raw:
The distri¬ 
bution of pele towers clearly shows the areas of vulnerability.

chapter_title: part m, 459-98, 507-8. For a list of Lake District place-names see LDH 81-101!
text: Towers lie thick along the Border, where the Englishman’s home had to be his castle.
text_raw:
Towers lie thick along the Border, where the Englishman’s home 
had to be his castle.

chapter_title: part m, 459-98, 507-8. For a list of Lake District place-names see LDH 81-101!
text: Another line, along the Solway, marks the crossings where low tides helped attack and hindered pursuit.
text_raw:
Another line, along the Solway, marks the 
crossings where low tides helped attack and hindered pursuit.

chapter_title: part m, 459-98, 507-8. For a list of Lake District place-names see LDH 81-101!
text: Further concentrations occur between the waste lands of Ingle¬ wood and Whinfell forests and the settlements of the Eden valley, and deep in the heart of the region pele towers on the lonely fells protected settlements far from the towns and gar¬ risoned castles.
text_raw:
Further concentrations occur between the waste lands of Ingle¬ 
wood and Whinfell forests and the settlements of the Eden 
valley, and deep in the heart of the region pele towers on the 
lonely fells protected settlements far from the towns and gar¬ 
risoned castles.

chapter_title: part m, 459-98, 507-8. For a list of Lake District place-names see LDH 81-101!
text: In construction the builders of the pele towers depended rather on mass than ingenuity.
text_raw:
In construction the builders of the pele towers depended rather 
on mass than ingenuity.

chapter_title: part m, 459-98, 507-8. For a list of Lake District place-names see LDH 81-101!
text: Walls varied in thickness from about three feet in the smaller and later towers to as much as ten feet in the double tower of Howgill Castle.
text_raw:
Walls varied in thickness from about 
three feet in the smaller and later towers to as much as ten feet 
in the double tower of Howgill Castle.

chapter_title: part m, 459-98, 507-8. For a list of Lake District place-names see LDH 81-101!
text: The inner and outer skins were of squared masonry set in courses but the filling was rubble laid in clay mortar.
text_raw:
The inner and outer skins 
were of squared masonry set in courses but the filling was rubble 
laid in clay mortar.

chapter_title: part m, 459-98, 507-8. For a list of Lake District place-names see LDH 81-101!

text: EARLY HISTORY OF THE LAKE COUNTIES 35 ceiling, giving protection to the upper floors even if it were lost.
text_raw:
EARLY HISTORY OF THE LAKE COUNTIES 35 
ceiling, giving protection to the upper floors even if it were lost.

chapter_title: part m, 459-98, 507-8. For a list of Lake District place-names see LDH 81-101!
text: Other floors were of timber and in some instances the risk of timber on the ground floor was accepted.
text_raw:
Other floors were of timber and in some instances the risk of 
timber on the ground floor was accepted.

chapter_title: part m, 459-98, 507-8. For a list of Lake District place-names see LDH 81-101!
text: Spans were short, division walls of stone being used in the larger peles.
text_raw:
Spans were short, 
division walls of stone being used in the larger peles.

chapter_title: part m, 459-98, 507-8. For a list of Lake District place-names see LDH 81-101!
text: Roofs were sometimes flat and covered with lead but many towers appear to have had pitched roofs of shingles or slates.
text_raw:
Roofs were 
sometimes flat and covered with lead but many towers appear to 
have had pitched roofs of shingles or slates.

chapter_title: part m, 459-98, 507-8. For a list of Lake District place-names see LDH 81-101!
text: Access to the pele towers of Cumberland and Westmorland was generally by the ground floor, which marks a difference from the Scottish peles, the Norman keeps and indeed many peles on the east of the Pennines, in which access was by ladder or staircase to the first floor.
text_raw:
Access to the pele 
towers of Cumberland and Westmorland was generally by the 
ground floor, which marks a difference from the Scottish peles, 
the Norman keeps and indeed many peles on the east of the 
Pennines, in which access was by ladder or staircase to the first 
floor.

chapter_title: part m, 459-98, 507-8. For a list of Lake District place-names see LDH 81-101!
text: Communication between floors was by a stone spiral stair¬ case arranged so as to present the vulnerable side of a single attacker to the defence.
text_raw:
Communication between floors was by a stone spiral stair¬ 
case arranged so as to present the vulnerable side of a single 
attacker to the defence.

chapter_title: part m, 459-98, 507-8. For a list of Lake District place-names see LDH 81-101!
text: The same staircase usually ran from the ground to the roof though sometimes it was broken on the first floor.
text_raw:
The same staircase usually ran from the 
ground to the roof though sometimes it was broken on the first 
floor.

chapter_title: part m, 459-98, 507-8. For a list of Lake District place-names see LDH 81-101!
text: The principal or only fireplace was on the first floor, hi early peles the fire may have been in the centre of the room, safe on the stone vaulted floor, but surviving towers have conventional fireplaces in the wall.
text_raw:
The principal or only fireplace was on the first floor, hi 
early peles the fire may have been in the centre of the room, safe 
on the stone vaulted floor, but surviving towers have conventional 
fireplaces in the wall.

chapter_title: part m, 459-98, 507-8. For a list of Lake District place-names see LDH 81-101!
text: Windows and doors increased in size and convenience as chances of attack diminished and means of glazing improved.
text_raw:
Windows and doors increased in size and 
convenience as chances of attack diminished and means of glazing 
improved.

chapter_title: part m, 459-98, 507-8. For a list of Lake District place-names see LDH 81-101!
text: Architectural embellishment generally was sparse and rude as befits structures intended as much for defence as habitation.
text_raw:
Architectural embellishment generally was sparse and 
rude as befits structures intended as much for defence as habitation.

chapter_title: part m, 459-98, 507-8. For a list of Lake District place-names see LDH 81-101!
text: Hardly any true pele towers survive, most of them having been incorporated in larger and more convenient dwellings.
text_raw:
Hardly any true pele towers survive, most of them having been

text: THE SIXTEENTH CENTURY IN LAKELAND (i) Politics and Religion The life of Lakeland, as we have endeavoured to describe it in the previous chapter, was still medieval in 1500, but the transition to modern times had been made, or at any rate well begun, when Elizabeth I died in 1603.
text_raw:
THE SIXTEENTH CENTURY IN LAKELAND (i) 
Politics and Religion 
The life of Lakeland, as we have endeavoured to describe it in 
the previous chapter, was still medieval in 1500, but the transition 
to modern times had been made, or at any rate well begun, when 
Elizabeth I died in 1603.

text: In one sense the Middle Ages might be regarded as coming to an end by 1540, by which time monastic life and ideals had, for the time at least, disappeared; in another sense the watershed between medieval and modern times might be dated in 1570, with the collapse of the northern rebellion, an event which made possible the effective integration of the northern counties in a realm dominated by the monarchy.
text_raw:
In one sense the Middle Ages might be 
regarded as coming to an end by 1540, by which time monastic 
life and ideals had, for the time at least, disappeared; in another 
sense the watershed between medieval and modern times might 
be dated in 1570, with the collapse of the northern rebellion, an 
event which made possible the effective integration of the 
northern counties in a realm dominated by the monarchy.

text: The establishment of the Society of Mines Royal at about the same time may be regarded as foreshadowing the mining and metal¬ lurgical importance which these counties were to attain in the following centuries.
text_raw:

lurgical importance which these counties were to attain in the

text: The major problems of the transition period may be reduced to three, one mainly political, a second mainly religious and a third essentially economic; but the story is greatly complicated by the interdependence of these three, for the political question had its religious and economic aspects, and the revolution in religion had economic and social consequences.

text: The Border Problem The political problem arose mainly from two circumstances, the geographical situation of the northern counties and the per¬ sistence in them of powerful noble families without whom they could not be governed effectively in 1500; but that very fact tended to produce what the advisers of Henry VIII and Elizabeth I could not but see, and detest, as an imperium in imperio.

text: That was because they commonly held their tenements by a customary tenant-right, varying somewhat from one manor to another but a tenure ‘tantamount to freehold’.3 As instances of tenants probably or certainly of this kind there may be cited, first, Richard Tolnson, of Burton in Kendal, who in L536 left his fermehold, after the death of his wife, to his younger daughter, then to the elder one, with remainder to the next of his name, by licence of the lord.4 A second was John Fawcett, of Over Kellet, who, in 1557, willed that Margaret his wife should have and occupy his farmhold during her life: he mentions a bond into which he had entered whereby his wife and two others were to occupy the tenement ‘to ye behoyf of my wyf and my chylder’ and to discharge the bond at ‘discrecion and lysans of ye lord of ye sed farmyhold’.5 A third example occurs in the will, dated 1542,® of Edmund Pereson, of Beetham.

text: In 1563 the Bishop of Carlisle was required by the government to supply answers to a series of questions, the fifth of which was ‘howe many howsholdes are within everie parishe, or within any suche member of any parishe that hath suche churches or chappells of ease?’1 The answers for the rural deaneries of Car¬ lisle (except Lanercost and Walton), Allerdale, Cumberland and Westmorland are extant, and the 72 Cumberland parishes or chapelries included then contained, according to the document, 6,162 households, which suggests a population of 27,729 or 30,810, according as to whether the average household be taken to have contained 4^ or 5 persons.

In 1563 the Bishop of Carlisle was required by the government 
to supply answers to a series of questions, the fifth of which was

30,810, according as to whether the average household be taken

text: Each of the 15 manors had a separate bailiff and all these officers were ‘under the com¬ mand of the land serjeant of Gilsland, as principal officer and mar¬ shall steward’.1 The manorial courts were held, in the eighteenth century and perhaps earlier, in the little market town of Bramp¬ ton.2 No account whatever of tenurial customs is given in the Survey, but the vast majority of the tenants held by tenant-right, despite the attempt of Lord William Howard to put an end to it.3 A remarkable feature of Gilsland is the great extent of common land.

text: Recent research shows that they reached their maximum extent about 1600 and that they can be proved to have existed in at least 220 townships out of 288 in Cumberland, where at one time they covered about one-sevendi of the total area.1 They can be traced not only in Gilcrux, Hesket, Ainstable, Croglin, Castle Carrock, Cumrew and Warwick, parishes where they could still be seen in 1795, and in Greystoke, Penruddock, Motherby and Torpenhow, where they still existed in the early nineteenth cen¬ tury, but also in Threlkeld, Mardale, Wet Sleddale, Northscale and Salthouse (then in Dalton parish), Broughton in Furness, Subberthwaite and Coniston.2 Clear traces of an ancient field arrangement and way of farm¬ ing are to be found in the part of the 1578 Survey relating to Aspatria.

text: It is clear from such information as we have that, as might be expected, prices of corn fluctuated within any one year according to the distance from harvest times, the character of the harvests and, no doubt, the largeness or smallness of stocks remaining from the previous year.
text_raw:
It is clear from such information as we have that, as might be 
expected, prices of corn fluctuated within any one year according 
to the distance from harvest times, the character of the harvests 
and, no doubt, the largeness or smallness of stocks remaining from 
the previous year.

text: There is some indication that the trend in wheat prices from 1612 to 1640 was downward; from 1640 to 1674 rather upward than downward; and from 1675 to 1699 slightly downward.1 There were no currency disturbances of the magni¬ tude of those experienced in the sixteenth century; but currency difficulties were great enough to lead to rioting in the Kendal region in 1696 and greatly hindered buying and selling among farmers as among other people.2 The major cause of fluctuation was very probably the weather.
text_raw:
There is some indication that the trend in 
wheat prices from 1612 to 1640 was downward; from 1640 to 1674 
rather upward than downward; and from 1675 to 1699 slightly 
downward.1 There were no currency disturbances of the magni¬

difficulties were great enough to lead to rioting in the Kendal 
region in 1696 and greatly hindered buying and selling among 
farmers as among other people.2 The major cause of fluctuation 
was very probably the weather.

text: Bad as the roads leading to them often were, Penrith, Kendal and the smaller market towns were probably active enough for the needs of the local population. ‘Its a Long way for ye market people to goe’, said Celia Fiennes about Penrith, ‘but they and their horses are used to it and go with much more facility than strangers.’1 Moreover it is clear that local shortages could to some extent be made good by commodities brought from a distance, and the transport conditions were good enough to enable some farmers at least to buy and sell in distant places.
text_raw:
Bad as the roads leading to them often were, Penrith, Kendal 
and the smaller market towns were probably active enough for 
the needs of the local population. ‘Its a Long way for ye market 
people to goe’, said Celia Fiennes about Penrith, ‘but they and 
their horses are used to it and go with much more facility than 
strangers.’1 Moreover it is clear that local shortages could to some 
extent be made good by commodities brought from a distance, 
and the transport conditions were good enough to enable some 
farmers at least to buy and sell in distant places.

text: The Swarthmoor household bought and sold not only in the local markets of Ulver- ston and Dalton but in Ravenglass, Hawkshead, Ambleside, Milnthorpe, Hornby, Kirkby Lonsdale, Lancaster and Preston.2 In 1674 it was concerned in buying wheat and bigg on a relatively large scale for export by sea to Bristol and also corn for Liverpool.3 In 1677 another venture of the same kind, this time to Cornwall, was organized.

In 1674 it was concerned in buying wheat and bigg on a relatively 
large scale for export by sea to Bristol and also corn for Liverpool.3 
In 1677 another venture of the same kind, this time to Cornwall, 
was organized.

text: The statute of 1390 exempted the poor northern cloth from the requirement to conform to fixed dimensions and by further sta¬ tutes in 1407 and 1410 the vendors were freed from the obligation to have such cloths sealed officially and to pay for the sealing.1 It is not clear how far these exemptions were annulled by a statute of 1597,2 the purpose of which was to reform abuses alleged to be ruining the reputation of northern cloths, especially the over-stretching of cloths on tenters by means of winches.
text_raw:
The statute of 1390 exempted the poor northern cloth from the 
requirement to conform to fixed dimensions and by further sta¬ 
tutes in 1407 and 1410 the vendors were freed from the obligation 
to have such cloths sealed officially and to pay for the sealing.1 
It is not clear how far these exemptions were annulled by a 
statute of 1597,2 the purpose of which was to reform abuses 
alleged to be ruining the reputation of northern cloths, especially 
the over-stretching of cloths on tenters by means of winches.

text: Accordingly provision was made for official searching by persons appointed by the justices of the peace or the municipal authorities and for punishing the offenders and destroying the prohibited contrivances.3 The malpractices nevertheless continued, so that in August 1600, and again in May 1601, the Privy Council sent letters to the justices of Yorkshire, Westmorland and Lancashire exhorting them to see that the Act was observed,4 but since letters to the same effect were directed also to the justices of Devon, Middlesex, Surrey, Salop and Wales we may take it that northern clothiers were not alone guilty.

text: A statute of 1609 declared that the Act of 1597 did not apply to ‘Kendals and other coarse things of like nature and made of the like coarse wool and differing in name only, called Cogware, coarse Cottons and Carptmeals’, and accordingly such cloths, produced in Cumberland, Westmorland, Cartmel, Hawkshead and Broughton in Furness might be made ‘in such sort as may best please the buyer’ as to dimensions, and were not to be subject to searching or sealing.5 This immunity from state regulation no doubt conduced to the expansion of the industry but at the same time it may have tended to hinder progress, for the exemptions would not apply if the clothiers were to attempt the making of finer fabrics, using better wool, which apparently was not to be obtained locally.
text_raw:
A statute of 1609 declared that the 
Act of 1597 did not apply to ‘Kendals and other coarse things of 
like nature and made of the like coarse wool and differing in name 
only, called Cogware, coarse Cottons and Carptmeals’, and 
accordingly such cloths, produced in Cumberland, Westmorland, 
Cartmel, Hawkshead and Broughton in Furness might be made 
‘in such sort as may best please the buyer’ as to dimensions, and 
were not to be subject to searching or sealing.5 
This immunity from state regulation no doubt conduced to the 
expansion of the industry but at the same time it may have tended 
to hinder progress, for the exemptions would not apply if the 
clothiers were to attempt the making of finer fabrics, using better 
wool, which apparently was not to be obtained locally.

text_raw:
LOCAL GOVERNMENT IN TUDOR AND 
STUART TIMES 
In the Lake Counties as elsewhere it is necessary to distinguish 
between local government and local self-government and to 
remember that self-government does not necessarily mean demo¬ 
cratic government.

text: In one sense the medieval organs for the maintenance of law and order, the sheriff and the county and hundred courts, were local, their jurisdictions being limited geographically; but in another sense they were organs of central government, since their purpose was to make the royal will effective in the areas subject to their authority.
text_raw:
In one sense the medieval organs for the 
maintenance of law and order, the sheriff and the county and 
hundred courts, were local, their jurisdictions being limited 
geographically; but in another sense they were organs of central 
government, since their purpose was to make the royal will 
effective in the areas subject to their authority.

text: There was thus the possibility of conflict between the authorities, who hoped to gam financially or at least not to lose much, and the inhabitants, who were not too willing to obey what they regarded as an external power and resented what they considered unjustifiable exactions.

Parish Business 
By Acts of 1555, 1562 and 15751 the ancient obligation of the 
inhabitants to keep highways in repair was reinforced and a 
system of road maintenance created.

text: A surveyor or surveyors of highways, unpaid and holding office for a year, had to be appointed in each parish and under the direction of such officers the house¬ holders might be compelled to turn out for six days a year at need to work on the roads, though they might send others in their place or agree with the surveyor to pay money instead.

A surveyor or surveyors of 
highways, unpaid and holding office for a year, had to be appointed 
in each parish and under the direction of such officers the house¬ 
holders might be compelled to turn out for six days a year at 
need to work on the roads, though they might send others in 
their place or agree with the surveyor to pay money instead.

text: In 1672, for example, it was ordered that a ‘poor, indigent, feeble old man’ in Holm Cultram should ‘goe from house to house and at every horse place 2 days, at every Demy foot place and lessor one day, according to a former neighbourly Rule, there to accept of such reliefe as shall be afforded him’.4 This method was commonly used in Allithwaite and other places in Lancashire north of the Sands.5 Another, often used in the same region, was a small cash pension.6 In Holm Cultram, where also such payments were made, the amount in 1670 and 1698 was usually nd. a week, later reduced to 6d.

text: POST-REFORMATION RELIGION AND CULTURE (2) Education The Schools The influence of the church upon the people, or at least upon a considerable part of them, was maintained not only by its services but also by means of something approaching monopoly in the education of the young, and the purpose of such education, as it was commonly conceived, was not so much positive—the widen¬ ing and hberating of the mind—as negative—the prevention of irreligious or anti-social conduct.

text: In Cartmel the master, according to a resolution in 1789: in summer shall go to school at six o’clock in the morning, and come to break¬ fast, and allow one hour for breakfast, and then return to school and stay till twelve noon, and go into school at two o’clock in the afternoon and stay till six o’clock in the evening; and in winter shall go into school at eight o’clock in the morning, and to have their breakfast before they come to school, and stay till twelve o’clock at noon, and in the afternoon shall go to school at one o’clock and stay till five in the evening; and shall only allow Saturdays for holidays, and shall not keep any red letter days as holidays, except one week at Easter, a fortnight holiday at Whitsuntide, and one month at Christmas.2 In Penridi, during both summer and winter, school started at six in the morning and finished at six at night, half an hour being allowed for breakfast and an hour for dinner.3 In village schools the period of instruction was perhaps not so long.

her education in the village school but she had means to visit 
London, Scotland and Ireland, and her sister married Colonel

station, she was familiar with the lives, hopes and fears of farmers 
and labourers in her neighbourhood and was often seen at their 
‘merrie neets’.

text: His method was, to drain and manure 1,000 acres fit for tillage, grass or meadow land; then build villages, consisting of eight or ten houses, with the necessary outbuildings, allotting to each so many acres, and then letting them to the most industrious among his married neigh¬ bours, frequently rent-free, for one or two years, or until they were able to pay rent. . . this worthy member of society so improved this part of the country, from a cold moist clay, heath and peat-land, that it is now the garden of that part of the country, and wears the appearance of the most improved soil about the metropolis.3 In this policy he was followed by his son, Sir James Graham, and his example in turn was copied by Lord Lonsdale.4 Sir Henry Fletcher, it is said, improved on Graham’s method of draining, greatly reducing the expense.5 The greatest of the reformers, however, was John Christian Curwen (1756-1828).6 He was a friend of Arthur Young and acquainted with the leaders of agricultural opinion in progressive Scotland, Lord Karnes and Sir John Sinclair; he travelled widely in Britain and on the Con¬ tinent, observing different ways of farming; and he apphed to the pursuit of agriculture something of the enterprise, technological interest and business capacity which distinguished him as a coal- owner.

text: Is it any wonder that the labourer has become pauperised?1 A similar point was made by the kindly Quaker, Thomas Wilkinson of Yanwath, with regard to the proposed enclosure of the small common of ioo acres or so on Yanwath Moor in 1812.2 He was no revolutionary. ‘I have mostly found rich men the most reasonable,’ he said, ‘I also fear society would be a sad loser generally if the rich and the poor were to change places.’ He was prepared to concede the advantage of enclosure in other instances, but with regard to this one he did not believe that the small additions which would be made to the holdings of the participants would compensate for the loss of the common:

text: Ofmeat, too, they had very little. ‘They subsisted chiefly’, says Gough, ‘on porridge made of oatmeal or dressed barley boiled in milk’.2 Potatoes, by the end of the century, were in common use, especially, according to Eden, ‘scraped raw, chopped and boiled together with a small quantity of meat cut into very small pieces. . . then formed into a hash with pepper, salt, onions See. . . by sailors called lobscouse’.3 In general, Eden believed, the northern labourers consumed a greater variety of foods, especially soups, than those of the south; and cheaper fuel made it possible for them to enjoy hot meals more often than their kind in the south ‘habituated to the unvarying meal of dry bread and cheese from week’s end to week’s end’.4 Nevertheless, though the Cumber¬ land and Westmorland labourers may have had these advantages, their diet, especially in winter, was often too poor, according to Gough, to enable them to resist diseases such as ague and was deficient in ‘esculent vegetables’.5 In the Kendal region, Eden thought, the labourers were apt to distribute their incomes unwisely, spending too little on sub¬ stantial food and too much on ale;6 but in this respect too the northern labourer was in general superior.

northern labourer was in general superior.

text: In the North, on the contrary, almost every article of dress worn by farmers, mechanics and labourers, is manufactured at home . . . there are many respectable persons, at this day, who never wore a bought pair of stockings, a coat nor waistcoat in their lives.4 This had certainly been true earlier, as Gough makes clear; but he also notes that one old-fashioned article of clothing, the ‘hard sark’ or shirt woven of hemp yarn, had long been in disrepute, and that the growing of flax was little practised in the Kendal region, where the women no longer knew how to spin linen yarn.5 By the time he was writing there was so great an aversion to home-spun cloth garments that the poor bought ‘a kind of second-hand finery from dealers in old clothes’.

text: A newer method, known as ‘long wall’, originating in Shropshire, was indeed used at Whar- nell Fell, Sebergham, soon after 1750; but this, which enabled all the coal in a seam to be got out in one operation, did not reach Whitehaven until 1870.2 It was probably not suitable in such deep pits, with an enormous weight above the workings, where, accordingly, very substantial support for the roof was required, namely pillars of coal ‘three yards high and about twelve yards square at the base’.3 The difficulties here, in addition to that en¬ countered in raising coal from so great a depth, were those com¬ monly met elsewhere, namely explosive and suffocating gases and problems of drainage.

text: Ten years earlier 21 men and a woman had been killed in a pit at Arrowthwaite.2 Water was at one time drawn, and coal was raised, from the pits by means of a gin or drum made to revolve by a horse, so that by means of a rope coiled or uncoiled around it corves or buckets could be lifted or lowered; but in 1715 a Newcomen ‘fire engine’ was hired and subsequently other engines were acquired, so that by 1777 there were four at work, capable of discharging 1,228 gallons of water a minute, or over one and three-quarter million gallons every twenty-four hours.3 Whether the later engines were of the improved kind made by Boulton and Watt is not clear from the remarks of Nicolson and Burn, though that is probable.

text: So far as is known, no tradesman in our region during the eighteenth century relieved the shortage by issuing token coins; but the partners in the Crake Mill at Spark Bridge in Furness in the 1790s appear to have issued their own notes or promises to pay on demand.1 Obligations to a firm’s suppliers were more generally met by bills: a manufacturer would be in possession of bills drawn on those to whom he had sold goods and could use these bills to pay people to whom he was himself indebted.
text_raw:
So far as is known, no tradesman in our region 
during the eighteenth century relieved the shortage by issuing 
token coins; but the partners in the Crake Mill at Spark Bridge 
in Furness in the 1790s appear to have issued their own notes or 
promises to pay on demand.1 Obligations to a firm’s suppliers 
were more generally met by bills: a manufacturer would be in 
possession of bills drawn on those to whom he had sold goods 
and could use these bills to pay people to whom he was himself 
indebted.

text: Many members probably rarely or never attended a meeting of the trust, and it is significant that five (or, for some purposes, seven) con¬ stituted a quorum.1 The construction of roads and of bridges and embankments, where necessary, was commonly let out to contract, and it sometimes happened that a contractor became road surveyor for the trustees.2 Meanwhile, the existence of the trusts did not end the legal obligation of the parishes to maintain their highways; and, with the consent of the justices, the statutory days of unpaid labour could, until 1835, be performed under the supervision of the trust surveyor, or the parishes could pay a composition instead.3 The establishment of turnpike trusts in our area began soon after 1750, the first being in 1752 for the road from Kendal through Kirkby Lonsdale to Keighley, and the second, in 1753, for the continuation northwards, from the Westmorland county boundary, of a road from the south: it ran from Heron Syke through Kendal and Shap to Eamont Bridge.

text: 1 The Tourists The tourist traffic, which today is of no small concern to the Lake District, did not begin until the second half of the eighteenth century.

1 
The Tourists 
The tourist traffic, which today is of no small concern to the 
Lake District, did not begin until the second half of the eighteenth 
century.

text: Occasional travellers, such as Celia Fiennes, had indeed ventured earlier into the district but it was terra incognita to most people south of the Trent or even the Mersey; and Defoe noted that its hills ‘high and formidable . . . had a kind of an unhospit- able terror in them’, while Westmorland was ‘a country eminent only for being the wildest, most barren and frightful ... in England, or even in Wales itself’.2 There were, indeed, several reasons why a widespread interest in the Lake Counties and a desire to visit them were late in developing.3 It may have been known that, despite the union of England and Scotland, public order and security were imperfectly established in the Border region, and, though highway robbery was common enough even in the neighbourhood of London itself, it may well have been thought, especially after the Jacobite rising of 1715, that life and property were far less safe in districts so near to Scotland.

text: Joseph Milburn, aged 12, was bound in 1804 to a Great Salkeld tailor till he should be 18; and James Grattan, aged 13, was apprenticed in 1809 to a Kirkoswald weaver for seven years.2 The conditions laid down in indentures of apprenticeship were probably similar in all districts and may be illustrated by a Wigton document of 1712.3 This stipulates that the apprentice during his term was not to resort to taverns, inns or alehouses, nor to play at cards, dice or other unlawful games; he was to submit himself to his master and not to be absent by day or night; and for any mis¬ demeanour he should yield his body for reasonable chastisement.

text: Buildings are neat, and many of them genteel; the shops exhibit a degree of elegance not often met with in the north: the houses are in general covered with blue slate, which gives the town a beautiful appearance from the adjoining heights.3 Maryport, hardly in existence in 1750, was by 1831 a town of over 3,800 inhabitants and could be described in 1811 as ‘neat and modern built . . . the streets . . . open and the situation healthy’.4 Workington, it is true, was then ‘a narrow and irregularly built town’, but it could be added in 1829 that ‘several of the modern streets are spacious and contain handsome buildings, so that the town is as agreeable as most others of a similar rank’.5 It was no doubt possible for the main streets and centre of a town to be open and airy while beyond and around them the inhabitants were crowded into mean houses in narrow alleys which visitors did not penetrate; but there is some ground for believing that, with one or two exceptions, the towns of our region, however defective in other respects, were not desperately overcrowded.

Maryport, hardly in existence in 1750, was by 1831 a town of over

text: In Kendal a picturesque relic of an older day, New- biggin, which obstructed the increasing traffic in Highgate, was swept away in 1803, and the completion of the Lancaster-Kendal canal in 1819 was followed by a good deal of house-building, aided by the Union Building Society.1 The motive of that society, according to tradition, was not merely to increase housing: the promoters were anti-Lowther in politics and the house-owners were qualified to vote in the county election, so that only ‘true Blues’ found accommodation in what were still known in the late nineteenth century as ‘Blue Buildings’.2 In Kirkby Lonsdale most of the houses were rebuilt and the streets and market place greatly improved.

text: There were no fewer than 300 street lamps by 1794, and by 1829 it could be said that ‘all the streets, lanes and outlets are well paved and lighted, and a nightly watch has been established, with police officers as a protection to the property and peace of the inhabitants’.4 In Carlisle, with coal available at a distance of only about 20 miles, gas lighting was used from 1819 onwards not only for the streets but for shops, factories and some private houses.

text: Both bodies were empowered to levy a rate up to a shilling in the pound.1 The Police Act of 1827 was probably thought necessary, in part at least, because of the unrest among textile workers in the district,2 many of them immigrants from Scotland and Ireland, and especially the weavers, crowded together in the poorer parts of the city and suburbs, such, for example, as Caldewgate, where in 1797 about a third of the population was receiving poor-relief.3 The cotton spinners in 1810 sympathized with distressed members of their trade in the Manchester region and sent contributions to aid men on strike there, and in 1812 delegates from Carlisle were present at a Manchester meeting the purpose of which was to press for the enforcement of old laws relating to apprenticeship and assessment of wages.

text: In 1816, for example, at Greystoke court leet, Tom Rumney of Mellfell and others, present in order to be admitted to their holdings, re¬ fused to pay the fines 011 the ground that the admittances, prepared beforehand, contained the words ‘at the will of the lord’, implying a right to exact arbitrary fines, and the words were erased when it had been shown that, according to the record in the Court Book, the fines ought to be by custom fixed, or ‘certain’.2 On the accession of the second Earl of Lonsdale the tenants of some of his manors refused to pay the arbitrary fines demanded, and it was decided by a suit in Chancery that they were to pay a ‘fine cer¬ tain’ of 10 times the rent and could enfranchise their holdings by paying 25 years’ purchase.3 These payments, or at any rate the ‘fines certain’, may not in fact have been so onerous as they seem, for, if the rents were the ancient, customary rents, they had, through the fall in the value of money, become very small; and the fines, if levied once every 10 or 20 years, may not have meant an inordinate addition to the annual rent.

text: Leisure Activities Having given some account of the Lake Counties population at home and at work, we may now, in order to make possible a general view of the nature of civilization in the region, indicate some of the people’s leisure activities and relaxations.

Having given some account of the Lake Counties population 
at home and at work, we may now, in order to make possible a 
general view of the nature of civilization in the region, indicate 
some of the people’s leisure activities and relaxations.

text: It should be understood that for most men and women, except in times of industrial depression, there was far less leisure than the ordinary person now has, and holidays were few.

text: The apparatus employed for amusement was less intricate and expensive and the organiza¬ tion of relaxation was far less elaborate than in these days of holiday camps, football cup finals and television, so that people were more dependent on their own initiative and on domestic or local resources than they are now; but it is to be noted that then, as in our own day, the popular taste was largely for contests involving physical strength or skill and in diversions providing opportunities for betting.

text: Certainly in 1656 the puritan ministers of Cumberland and Westmorland regarded football and wrestling as, if not wrong in themselves, certainly wrong on Sundays.1 By the early nineteenth century the special Cumberland and Westmorland hold and method, practised also in Northumberland and Furness, had been developed and were used in the annual competitions which were held in many villages, the victor’s prize commonly being an ornate belt.
text_raw:
Certainly in 1656 the puritan ministers of Cumberland 
and Westmorland regarded football and wrestling as, if not 
wrong in themselves, certainly wrong on Sundays.1 By the early 
nineteenth century the special Cumberland and Westmorland 
hold and method, practised also in Northumberland and Furness, 
had been developed and were used in the annual competitions 
which were held in many villages, the victor’s prize commonly 
being an ornate belt.

text: At the opening of the century the wrestlers of Cumberland, and especially of the Carlisle and Penrith regions, were in greater repute than those of south Westmorland; but it is beheved that from about 1809 onwards die sport was stimulated in the Ambleside district by John Wilson, then living at Elleray, and wrestling matches for money prizes became added attractions at race meetings.
text_raw:
At the opening of the century the wrestlers 
of Cumberland, and especially of the Carlisle and Penrith regions, 
were in greater repute than those of south Westmorland; but it is 
beheved that from about 1809 onwards die sport was stimulated 
in the Ambleside district by John Wilson, then living at Elleray, 
and wrestling matches for money prizes became added attractions 
at race meetings.

text: Horse racing, carried on in the sixteenth century at Lang- wathby and on Kingsmoor near Carlisle, seems to have increased in popularity, for in Stuart times there were racecourses near Drigg, Westward, Skinburness, Hesket in the Forest, Parton, Workington and Burgh by Sands, and in the eighteenth century at Penrith, Wigton, Egremont, and other places including Lady- field, near Kendal, where, however, racing ceased about 1790, to be revived in 1820.2 Lord Lowther was present on that occasion and no doubt the sport appealed greatly to the gentry, owners of horses and generally given to wagering, but it was not without its attraction also for town dwellers, at any rate those of Carlisle.

text: Secondly, society was more secure against raids and violence from without and rebellion from within; it had a much safer margin against famine and much better means of dealing with poverty and destitution.

There is a kind of sheep in these mountains called Herdwicks which, when 
properly fed to the highest growth seldom exceed 9 or 10 lbs. a quarter.

text: They, contrary to all other sheep I have met with, are seen before a storm, especially of snow, to ascend against the coming blast and to take the stormy side of the mountain, which saves them from being overblown.
text_raw:
They, 
contrary to all other sheep I have met with, are seen before a storm, especially 
of snow, to ascend against the coming blast and to take the stormy side of the 
mountain, which saves them from being overblown.

text: This valuable instinct was first discovered by the people of Wasdalehead.
text_raw:
This valuable instinct was 
first discovered by the people of Wasdalehead.

text: They, to keep this breed as much as possible in their own village, bound themselves in a bond that no one should sell above 5 ewe or female lambs in one year.
text_raw:
They, to keep this breed as much 
as possible in their own village, bound themselves in a bond that no one should 
sell above 5 ewe or female lambs in one year.

text: But means were found to smuggle more, so that all the shepherds now have either the whole or half breed of them, especially where the mountains are very high, as in Borrowdale, Newlands and Skiddaw, where they have not hay for them in the winter.
text_raw:
But means were found to smuggle 
more, so that all the shepherds now have either the whole or half breed of them, 
especially where the mountains are very high, as in Borrowdale, Newlands and 
Skiddaw, where they have not hay for them in the winter.

text: These sheep lie upon the very tops of the mountains in winter as well as summer.
text_raw:
These sheep lie upon 
the very tops of the mountains in winter as well as summer.

text: If a calm snow fall, the shepherds take a harrow and drag it over the tallest heath or ling; the snow then falls to the bottom and the sheep feed upon the tops of it and upon the moss which grows upon stones.
text_raw:

heath or ling; the snow then falls to the bottom and the sheep feed upon the 
tops of it and upon the moss which grows upon stones.

text: Whence this breed first came I cannot learn.

text: APPENDIX II CORN AND LIVESTOCK PRICES It would be possible to accumulate from various sources a number of miscellaneous prices for com, vegetables, cattle, sheep and wool in our area, but it does not seem possible to construct any very useful series, for various reasons.
text_raw:
APPENDIX II 
CORN AND LIVESTOCK PRICES 
It would be possible to accumulate from various sources a number of 
miscellaneous prices for com, vegetables, cattle, sheep and wool in our 
area, but it does not seem possible to construct any very useful series, 
for various reasons.

text: One is the variety of goods: heifers, cows, calves, bulls and oxen varied in weight, quality and buyers’ estimation so much that an individual price record tells us very little, and there is the same difficulty with ewes, wethers, tups and lambs.
text_raw:
One is the variety of goods: heifers, cows, calves, 
bulls and oxen varied in weight, quality and buyers’ estimation so much 
that an individual price record tells us very little, and there is the same 
difficulty with ewes, wethers, tups and lambs.

text: In corn there were differ¬ ences of quality, and we cannot be sure that measures bearing the same name had the same capacity in different parts of our district.
text_raw:
In corn there were differ¬ 
ences of quality, and we cannot be sure that measures bearing the same 
name had the same capacity in different parts of our district.

text: The greatest difficulty, however, is the want of runs of prices in the same market for any considerable number of years.
text_raw:

difficulty, however, is the want of runs of prices in the same market for 
any considerable number of years.
